kurz: Why the price already contains the majority opinion, and why the stock market only pays for what goes beyond it.

bloecke.md:
The first order is the level at which most conversations about money take place. Typical sentences are “The company is growing, so I'm buying the share” and “Interest rates are falling, so prices will rise”. None of these sentences is wrong. But each one is incomplete, because it leaves out one quantity, namely the price, in which this thought is already contained.

Howard Marks, co-founder of Oaktree Capital, derived from this the distinction on which his entire body of work is built. First-order thinking asks whether a company is good. Second-order thinking asks whether it is better than the price assumes. The first question concerns the company, the second the difference between the company and the expectation. On the stock exchange, only this difference is paid for.

A price tells you about the market's expectation and not about the quality of a company. The return on a share depends on the gap between what the company will deliver and what the market already prices in.

This results in a strict condition. To do better than the market, being right is not enough. Your own opinion must differ from the majority and at the same time be correct; one alone is not enough. An investor who shares the majority opinion and turns out to be right gets the market return minus their own costs. That is a decent result, but it rests solely on being invested and is not an achievement of their own.

bloecke.unter: Deviation and correctness form two separate axes, and an edge only arises where the two coincide.

felder.text: Right, like everyone else. The result is the index minus costs. Solid, but without an edge, since the assessment had long been priced in.
A differing opinion that turns out to be correct. Only here does outperformance arise, and it ends the moment the rest of the market adopts the opinion.
You are wrong along with the market. Unpleasant, but with relatively few consequences, because the result is again roughly in line with the index.
The deviation brings a worse result and the experience that going it alone does not automatically mean foresight.

bloecke.md:
Finding it hard to stand against a majority is not a character flaw. In Solomon Asch's conformity experiments, 74% of the test subjects gave an obviously wrong answer at least once, only because the group had given it before them. When tested alone, the error rate was below 0.7%. With a differing, correct opinion, the difficulty rarely lies in the analysis. Usually it lies in holding on to the opinion while it still looks wrong.

How often the two come together is measured by the SPIVA scorecard from S&P Dow Jones Indices. In the European edition for mid-2025, 98.22% of euro-denominated global equity funds missed their benchmark index over ten years. This is the largest active category in Europe and thus the direct competitor to the ordinary world ETF. There is serious criticism of the method behind these analyses. In May 2026, Cremers, Fulkerson and Riley showed for US equity funds that the rate over 20 years falls to around 55% if you weight by assets instead of by number of funds, assess funds that were wound up on their performance until they were wound up and compare against actual index funds instead of against the index. The study was funded by the Active Managers Council. Even in this reading, which is more favourable to active funds, missing the benchmark is somewhat more likely than beating it.

bloecke.titel: Strategists' consensus forecast and outcome in two years
bloecke.unter: From 2018 to 2025, the consensus estimate of Wall Street strategists for the S&P 500 was within plus or minus ten percentage points in only one of eight years.

bloecke.md: Two things are often confused here. As a forecast, the consensus is poor. In 2022 the strategists expected plus 3.9%, and the result was minus 19.4%, that is, 23.3 percentage points off. As a price, however, the same consensus is hard to beat. The price is the point at which buyers and sellers with real money are in balance, and it is thus something other than the average of the forecasts. A better forecast than the strategists' therefore does not yet produce a profit. Only an assessment that proves the price wrong produces a profit.

## Company quality and share return

In psychology, the first-order thinking error is called the representativeness heuristic. In 1983, Tversky and Kahneman used the Linda problem to show that people confuse similarity with probability. Around 85% of respondents considered the more specific answer, which fitted the story better, to be the more probable one, although logically it cannot be. On the stock exchange, the same confusion shows up when a good company looks like a good investment.

Arithmetically, the price return over a long period breaks down into two factors. One is what the business earns, the other what the market is prepared to pay for it.

bloecke.formel: Final price / Initial price = (Earnings end / Earnings start) × (P/E end / P/E start)
bloecke.erklaerung: The first factor stands for the business, the second for the expectation. If the [[Price-to-earnings ratio (P/E)|price-to-earnings ratio]] falls from 45 to 18, the second factor is 0.40. Earnings growth must first make up for this decline before any return arises at all.
variablen: earnings per share, that is, net profit divided by the number of shares
price-to-earnings ratio, the price paid for one euro of annual profit

bloecke.titel: Illustrative calculation over ten years excluding dividends, costs and taxes
Earnings growth and price return per year in the model
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation: after ten years, the growth star earns three times as much and is nevertheless the worse share, because the expectation shrinks while earnings grow.

bloecke.md:
The model is not a verdict on growth shares. If the growth star keeps up its pace for twenty years instead of ten, or if its P/E only falls to 33 instead of 18, the result is reversed. What matters for the decision is therefore the assumption that is already contained in the price. Which company is better is not the deciding factor.

## Asking further, step by step

Second-order thinking can be applied as a chain of follow-up questions. Instead of evaluating a piece of news, you keep thinking through its consequences until nothing new emerges.

schritte.text: Note down only the news, without interpreting it. Example: the ECB cuts its key interest rate.
The first-order answer is that loans become cheaper and shares look relatively more attractive. That is usually true, but it is always already known.
If the cut had been priced in on the futures market for weeks, it is already in the price. The market is then only moved by the deviation from the expectation.

Rates are usually cut because the economy is weakening. Lower interest rates raise valuations, a weaker economy lowers profits. Which effect predominates is the decisive question, and it has no automatic answer.
Record what would have to be true for your own deviation to be right. If this cannot be put into one sentence, the differing opinion is just a feeling.

bloecke.titel: Selling because of a high valuation
bloecke.md:
The portfolio contains units of a globally investing equity ETF worth €30,000; the acquisition costs were €10,000. The valuation looks high, and the first-order reasoning is to sell and buy back lower.

The second-order calculation starts with tax. Realised gains from fund units are subject to [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] of 25% under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act) plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge, together 26.375%, and correspondingly more with church tax. For equity funds, 30% of the gain remains tax-free under Section 20(1) InvStG (Investment Tax Act). In this example, the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) under Section 20(9) EStG is assumed to have been used up. Advance lump sums (Vorabpauschalen) from previous years are left out; they would reduce the gain under Section 19(1) sentence 3 InvStG.

bloecke.titel: Minimum decline from which the sale pays off
zeilen: Flat-rate withholding tax plus solidarity surcharge, 26.375%
Price decline needed for the same number of units

bloecke.md: The price must therefore fall by more than 12.3% for you to hold more units after buying back than before. Moreover, this only holds if the buyback actually takes place. The first-order question was whether the investment is expensive. The second-order question is whether it is more than 12.3% too expensive and whether you trust yourself to know that. In addition, the tax deferral that builds up through long holding is used up for good after the sale.

This tool is most often misused as contrarianism at any price, that is, as a rule of always doing the opposite of the majority. That is first-order thinking again, just with the sign reversed. It assumes that the majority is usually wrong. But usually it is right, and that is why the market is hard to beat. Standing against the consensus is not a goal in itself. What Marks is concerned with is checking whether an opinion is already contained in the price. If it is, nothing can be earned from it, however right it may be.

In the first case, the claim is that the care market is certain to grow. In first-order terms, the ageing of Germany's population is the most reliable forecast there is, so you buy operators of care facilities. But the trend has featured in every plan for decades and is therefore in the price. Demand is known; what is open is who keeps the margin. Care fees are negotiated and regulated, and staff costs rise with the shortage of skilled workers. Secure demand without pricing power does not drive profit.

In the second case, a company reports a record profit, and the share price falls. In first-order terms, the market is irrational. But a record is a comparison with the past, whereas a price is a comparison with the expectation. The price fell because the outlook was weaker than what had been priced in.

In the third case, everyone is warning of a crash. In first-order terms, you hedge. But if the warning is general, the cautious are already being cautious, and part of the selling pressure is already behind the market. Marks' pendulum between greed and fear, however, only shows where you stand, not when it will swing back.

Before every active decision, write down a sentence following this pattern: *The market expects X, I expect Y, and I consider Y to be right because Z.* If you cannot formulate X, you do not know what you are betting against. Filed with the date, after twelve months the collection provides the only reliable information on whether the effort is worthwhile.

mitnehmen: A price reflects the market's expectation, and only the difference between this expectation and the quality of the company is paid for.
Outperformance requires an opinion that differs from the consensus and is also correct, and the base rates for this are unfavourable.
Earnings growth and price return can be far apart if the valuation multiple moves in the opposite direction.
The consensus is weak as a forecast and nevertheless hard to beat as a price.
In Germany, second-order thinking has a tax side, because tax is due immediately on realised gains, and buying back in first has to earn it back.

begriffe.text: Way of thinking, following Howard Marks, that examines whether something is better than the price already assumes, instead of merely asking whether it is good. Only the difference between reality and the priced-in expectation produces outperformance or underperformance.

The majority opinion about the future of a security that has already been processed into the market price. It forms the price and therefore brings no additional return. Only deviations from it move the price.
Decline in the valuation multiple, for example the P/E ratio, while profit stays the same or even rises. It can push the price return below profit growth for years.

Tax-exempt portion of the income from investment funds under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act). For privately held investments, it is 30% for equity funds and 15% for mixed funds with an equity ratio of at least 25%.
